issues.title: Python variable uses camelCase naming
issues.description: The rule requires all Python variables and functions to use snake_case naming convention, but the code uses camelCase for the variable 'escapedPattern' instead of 'escaped_pattern'
issues.problematic_code_snippet:
if not pattern:
        return pattern
    # Escape backslash first, then percent and underscore
    escapedPattern = pattern.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("%", "\\%").replace("_", "\\_")
    return escapedPattern
issues.rule_name: Python Code Must Use Snake Case for Variables and Functions

issues.title: Missing escape parameter in 'not contains' metadata filter
issues.description: In the metadata filtering logic for dataset retrieval, the 'not contains' case applies escape_like_pattern() to escape special characters but fails to specify the escape='\' parameter in the notlike() call. This renders the escaping ineffective - the database won't interpret the backslash escapes correctly, allowing special characters like %, _, and \ to be treated as SQL wildcards instead of literal characters. This creates a SQL injection vulnerability through LIKE wildcards and causes incorrect query results when filtering metadata that contains these special characters.

issues.title: Incorrect escape character in IRIS vector database LIKE query
issues.description: The IRIS vector database implementation escapes special characters using backslash (via escape_like_pattern which produces \%, \_, \\) but then specifies ESCAPE '|' in the SQL query instead of ESCAPE '\'. This mismatch causes the database to look for the wrong escape character - it will treat | as the escape character while the string contains backslash escapes. As a result, the escaped special characters won't be properly interpreted, allowing SQL wildcards to remain active and causing search queries with special characters to produce incorrect results or security vulnerabilities.
issues.problematic_code_snippet:
escaped_query = escape_like_pattern(query)
                query_pattern = f"%{escaped_query}%"
                sql = f"""
                    SELECT TOP {top_k} id, text, meta
                    FROM {self.schema}.{self.table_name}
                    WHERE text LIKE ? ESCAPE '|'
                """

issues.title: Keyword trimming logic may break escape sequences
issues.description: The workflow app service trims the keyword to 30 characters and then applies escape_like_pattern(). However, this creates a subtle bug: if a backslash character appears exactly at position 30, the trim could split an escape sequence that the user intended. More critically, if special characters appear in positions 28-30, they'll be included in the escaped output, but any context around them will be lost, potentially creating malformed escape sequences. The trimming should occur AFTER escaping to preserve the integrity of the escape sequences, or better yet, the escaping should be done before any string manipulation.
issues.problematic_code_snippet:
# Escape special characters in keyword to prevent SQL injection via LIKE wildcards
            keyword_trimmed = keyword[:30]
            escaped_keyword = escape_like_pattern(keyword_trimmed)
            keyword_like_val = f"%{escaped_keyword}%"

issues.title: Improper import ordering (isort/ruff)
issues.description: Ruff/isort requires standard-library imports to be sorted consistently. Here, `from unittest.mock ...` (module `unittest`) should be ordered before `import uuid` (module `uuid`) within the standard library import section.
issues.problematic_code_snippet:

from unittest.mock import create_autospec, patch

pr.title: Code Review Bench PR #30450 - fix(api): refactors the SQL LIKE pattern escaping logic to use a centralized utility function

structured_output.summary:
This PR adds `libs.helper.escape_like_pattern()`, which backslash-escapes `\`, `%` and `_`. It then uses that helper, together with `escape="\\"`, at every user-facing LIKE/ILIKE call site: console conversation search, segment and child-chunk search, annotations, apps, datasets, external knowledge APIs, tags, workflow logs, metadata filters, and the ClickZetta and IRIS vector fallbacks. Centralising the helper is the right idea, and most call sites are converted correctly. It also comes with unit tests and container integration tests.

Three call sites are wrong, though. The IRIS fallback declares `ESCAPE '|'` even though the helper escapes with a backslash, so any query containing `%`, `_` or `\` now returns wrong results. The workflow-log search drops the existing `unicode_escape` handling. Inputs and outputs are stored with `json.dumps` (ensure_ascii), so searching for any non-ASCII keyword, such as Chinese text, no longer finds anything. Finally, the metadata filter's `not contains` branch escapes the value but doesn't pass `escape=`, unlike the other three branches. The new tests don't cover any of these three paths.
structured_output.verdictRationale: Two regressions need fixing before merge: the IRIS escape character doesn't match what the helper produces, and workflow-log search no longer finds non-ASCII keywords. Both break searches that work today, and neither is caught by the tests.

architecture.overview:
User-supplied search strings come in through console controllers and service methods, and end up in SQLAlchemy `ilike`/`like` expressions or raw SQL in the vector-store adapters. Before this PR each call site put the raw keyword straight into `%...%`, so `%` and `_` acted as wildcards. Only `ConversationService` had its own inline escaping.

This PR adds one helper, `escape_like_pattern` in `libs/helper.py`, and routes every call site through it. Each site then tells the database that backslash is the escape character, either with SQLAlchemy's `escape="\\"` or with a raw `ESCAPE` clause. For the result to be correct, the escape character declared at each call site has to match what the helper produces, and the escaped value has to match how the column is stored (for example, JSON-encoded text in `WorkflowRun.inputs`).
steps: Start at `api/libs/helper.py::escape_like_pattern`. It escapes backslash first, then `%` and `_`, always using backslash as the escape character.

Look at the SQLAlchemy ORM call sites in services and controllers (`app_service`, `tag_service`, `annotation_service`, `dataset_service`, `external_knowledge_service`, `conversation.py`, `datasets_segments.py`). Each one wraps the escaped value in `%...%` and passes `escape="\\"`.
`dataset_retrieval.process_metadata_filter_func` applies the helper to the four LIKE-based metadata conditions: contains, not contains, start with and end with.

`workflow_app_service.get_paginate_workflow_app_logs` searches JSON-encoded `WorkflowRun.inputs`/`outputs` text and `EndUser.session_id`. The PR replaces the previous unicode-escape transform with the helper.
The raw-SQL vector adapters (`clickzetta_vector.py`, `iris_vector.py`) add their own `ESCAPE` clause to the LIKE fallback.

findings.title: IRIS LIKE fallback declares ESCAPE '|' but the helper escapes with backslash
findings.body:
`escape_like_pattern` always escapes with a backslash (`50%` becomes `50\%`). This query, however, tells IRIS that `|` is the escape character:

::diff{file="api/core/rag/datasource/vdb/iris/iris_vector.py" lines="290-300"}

With `ESCAPE '|'`, IRIS reads the backslash as an ordinary character, and the `%` or `_` after it is still a wildcard. Some examples:
- Query `50%` becomes the pattern `%50\%%`. It only matches text containing `50\` followed by anything, so a document containing `50% off` is **not** found.
- Query `test_data` becomes `%test\_data%`. It only matches a literal `test\` + one char + `data`.
- Any query with a backslash gets its backslashes doubled, so it never matches.

This is worse than the old behaviour. Previously these queries at least matched their own literal text, plus some extra wildcard matches. An earlier revision of this branch used `ESCAPE '\\'`, so this looks like an accidental change.

::suggestion{file="api/core/rag/datasource/vdb/iris/iris_vector.py" lines="298-298"}
                    WHERE text LIKE ? ESCAPE '\\'

(In Python source, `'\\'` produces the SQL literal `'\'`, a single backslash.)
findings.fixPrompt: In `api/core/rag/datasource/vdb/iris/iris_vector.py` around line 298, the LIKE fallback uses `ESCAPE '|'`. But `libs.helper.escape_like_pattern` escapes `%`, `_` and `\` with a backslash, so escaped wildcards are still treated as wildcards and literal searches fail. Change the escape clause to a single backslash (`ESCAPE '\\'` in the Python string, which is `ESCAPE '\'` in SQL) so it matches the helper. If possible, add a unit test that mocks the cursor and asserts the SQL and parameters passed to `cursor.execute`.

findings.title: Workflow log keyword search no longer matches non-ASCII text
findings.body:
The old code turned the keyword into its JSON `\uXXXX` form, because that's how `WorkflowRun.inputs` and `outputs` are stored. `SQLAlchemyWorkflowExecutionRepository` writes them with plain `json.dumps(...)` (line 152), which uses `ensure_ascii=True`. The PR deletes that transform:

::diff{file="api/services/workflow_app_service.py" lines="88-103"}

As a result, a search for `测试` now builds `%测试%`. The stored text is `{"q": "测试"}`, so the search **never matches** any input or output that contains Chinese, Japanese, emoji, accented characters, and so on. Dify has a large CJK user base, so this is a real regression. No test covers it: the new tests only use ASCII keywords.

The fix is to JSON-encode the keyword the same way the column is stored, then LIKE-escape the result. `session_id` isn't JSON-encoded, so it should keep using the plain escaped value:

::suggestion{file="api/services/workflow_app_service.py" lines="92-103"}
            keyword_trimmed = keyword[:30]
            # inputs/outputs are stored via json.dumps (ensure_ascii=True), so match their encoded form
            json_encoded_keyword = json.dumps(keyword_trimmed)[1:-1]
            json_like_val = f"%{escape_like_pattern(json_encoded_keyword)}%"
            plain_like_val = f"%{escape_like_pattern(keyword_trimmed)}%"
            keyword_conditions = [
                WorkflowRun.inputs.ilike(json_like_val, escape="\\"),
                WorkflowRun.outputs.ilike(json_like_val, escape="\\"),
                # filter keyword by end user session id if created by end user role
                and_(
                    WorkflowRun.created_by_role == "end_user",
                    EndUser.session_id.ilike(plain_like_val, escape="\\"),
                ),
            ]

A side benefit: this also handles `"` and `\` in the keyword correctly, because they're stored as `\"` and `\\` inside the JSON.
findings.fixPrompt: In `api/services/workflow_app_service.py` (lines ~88-103), the PR removed the `unicode_escape` transform of the keyword. `WorkflowRun.inputs` and `outputs` are written with `json.dumps` (ensure_ascii=True) in `api/core/repositories/sqlalchemy_workflow_execution_repository.py:152`, so non-ASCII keywords like Chinese no longer match. Build the inputs/outputs pattern from `json.dumps(keyword[:30])[1:-1]` and pass that through `escape_like_pattern`. Keep a separate plain escaped pattern for `EndUser.session_id`. Keep `escape="\\"` on all ilike calls. Add a container integration test in `api/tests/test_containers_integration_tests/services/test_workflow_app_service.py` that creates a WorkflowRun whose inputs contain Chinese text and asserts that searching for the Chinese keyword finds it.

findings.title: `not contains` metadata filter escapes the value but omits `escape=`
findings.fixPrompt: In `api/core/rag/retrieval/dataset_retrieval.py` line ~1207 (`process_metadata_filter_func`, the `not contains` case), add `escape="\\"` to the `json_field.notlike(...)` call so it matches the `contains`, `start with` and `end with` branches. Consider adding a unit test that compiles each filter and asserts the ESCAPE clause is present.

findings.title: New tests miss the risky paths and repeat the same assertion as 'Test 4'
findings.body:
In each new integration test, "Test 4" repeats Test 1's exact query (`keyword="50%"`) and assertion (`total == 1`), so it adds no coverage:

::diff{file="api/tests/test_containers_integration_tests/services/test_tag_service.py" lines="390-393"}

The same repetition appears in `test_annotation_service.py` (line 511) and `test_app_service.py` (line 1126). Meanwhile, the call sites most likely to go wrong have no tests:
- workflow-log search with non-ASCII text
- the IRIS and ClickZetta raw-SQL escape clauses
- the metadata `not contains` filter

A better negative test would search for `5_%` or `%different`. Without escaping, those would match more rows; with escaping, they match none. That actually shows the wildcards are treated literally.

Separately, `test_escape_none_handling` passes `None` to a function typed `pattern: str`. That locks in a behaviour the signature says is unsupported, and it will trip type checkers.
findings.fixPrompt: In the new special-character tests in `api/tests/test_containers_integration_tests/services/test_tag_service.py` (~line 390), `test_annotation_service.py` (~line 511) and `test_app_service.py` (~line 1126), 'Test 4' repeats Test 1 exactly. Replace it with a query that would over-match if escaping were broken, such as keyword `5_%` or `%different`, and assert it returns 0 results. In `api/tests/unit_tests/libs/test_helper.py`, either remove `test_escape_none_handling` or change the helper signature to `str | None` so the type and the test agree.

findings.title: Unexplained 'circular dependency' import rewrites in test files
findings.fixPrompt: In `api/tests/test_containers_integration_tests/services/test_app_service.py` and `test_workflow_app_service.py`, the PR replaces the top-level `from services.app_service import AppService` with many in-function imports, citing a circular dependency. Check whether the top-level import actually fails. If it doesn't, restore the single module-level import and remove the repeated local imports and commented-out lines. If it does, document the cycle and fix it in production code instead.

findings.title: camelCase local variable in helper
findings.fixPrompt: In `api/libs/helper.py` lines 64-65, replace the camelCase temporary `escapedPattern` with a direct `return` of the replace chain, following the project's snake_case and ruff conventions.

findings.title: Centralising LIKE escaping is a good consolidation
findings.body: Replacing the inline escape in `ConversationService` and the raw `f"%{keyword}%"` patterns spread across the codebase with a single helper is the right move. The helper escapes backslash first, which is the correct order, and the unit tests pin that ordering. Escaping is also applied *after* truncation in `app_service` (`[:30]`) and `workflow_app_service`, so truncation can't cut an escape sequence in half. Most ORM call sites consistently pass `escape="\\"`.
